**Y3 is feature 4.** In task X4-Y3-Z1, the output is 3 exactly when feature 4 has the same value in both stimuli. Otherwise it is 0. This leaves two readings:
- (A) X4 = "both are the same", with Z1 giving 3 when true and 0 when false.
- (B) X4 = "exactly one is 1", with Z1 giving 0 when true and 3 when false.

**Y4 is feature 2 and Y2 is feature 1.** In task X2-Y4-Z4, the output is 2 exactly when neither stimulus has feature 2. In tasks X2-Y2-Z3 and X2-Y2-Z2, the rare output (2 and 0 respectively) appears exactly when neither stimulus has feature 1. So X2 is one of two rules:
- (a) X2 = "at least one is 1". Then Z2 gives 1 when true and 0 when false.
- (b) X2 = "neither is 1". Then Z2 gives 0 when true and 1 when false.

**X5.** In task X5-Y3-Z2, the output is 1 exactly when neither stimulus has feature 4. Combined with Z2:
- Under (a), X5 = "neither is 1".
- Under (b), X5 = "at least one is 1".

Every combination keeps X2, X4 and X5 different from each other, so all four combinations fit the known tasks.

**Effect on the new task (X5-Y3-Z1).**
- Combinations aA and bB give: 3 when neither stimulus has feature 4, otherwise 0.
- Combinations aB and bA give the reverse: 0 when neither stimulus has feature 4, otherwise 3.

The examples cannot separate these, so I chose the aA/bB version. Inputs 2, 6, 9, 13 and 14 have feature 4 off in both stimuli, so they get 3. All other inputs get 0.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
